ce:section.ce:para: Polymeric adhesives that can bond two or more parts together have been widely used in many industries, such as wood, automotive, and medicine (Liu et al., 2020). Most commercial adhesives are based on non-renewable and depleting petrochemical resources (Chen et al., 2017; Patel, 2015; Zhang et al., 2019). Moreover, several adhesives also contain residual toxic chemicals and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) (Chen et al., 2017; Kim, 2009; Patel, 2015; Zhang et al., 2019). Due to their environmental impact or hazard to living organisms’ health, environmental protection organizations aim to reduce the usage of such materials (Patel, 2015; Pradyawong et al., 2018). These two problems seem to be overcome simultaneously by replacing the synthetic materials with natural resources (Parija et al., 2001) and taking advantage of water-based adhesives (Ahmadi-Dehnoei and Ghasemirad, 2021), which have gained a considerable deal of attention in a majority of industries, such as wood (Mabrouk et al., 2020), footwear (Orgilés-Calpena et al., 2019), and food packaging industries (Canellas et al., 2017). After drying, water-based synthetic adhesives could not be redispersed in water anymore; therefore, several techniques have been proposed for adhesive debonding with the aim of easy recycling and repairing of bonded structures (Banea, 2019; Liu et al., 2020). These strategies include usage of solvent, heat, light or incorporation of dynamic chemical bonds or fillers in the adhesive (Banea, 2019). Given that in the past few decades, about 65 % of adhesives have been used in the wood industry (Liu et al., 2020), the development of dismantlable adhesives is very important in this field. In this regard, efforts such as usage of thermally expandable nanoparticles or dynamic disulfide bonds in the adhesive formulations were made to develop dismantlable adhesives for interior furniture and wood boards (Ishikawa et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2020).

Polysaccharides, lignin, tannin, and proteins are examples of bio-based polymers with potential application in wood adhesives (Norström et al., 2014). Polysaccharides are the most abundant category of bio-based polymers made of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds. The high molecular weight of polysaccharides results in an acceptable cohesive strength of their adhesives. On the other hand, high contents of hydroxyl polar groups afford strong wood adhesion by creating hydrogen interactions. However, polysaccharide adhesives suffer from low water resistance due to their hydrophilic nature provided by high hydroxyl contents (Araújo et al., 2016). Therefore, in order to achieve suitable properties, their modification through blending or grafting with synthetic polymers, oxidation, esterification, crosslinking, or addition of inorganic nanoparticles is essential (Mati-Baouche et al., 2014; Norström et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2018). Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2012) reported shear strengths of 0.25, 2.29, and 3.65 MPa for gelatinized starch, 1:1 w/w blend of polyvinyl acetate and starch, and 1:1 w/w polyvinyl acetate-grafted starch, as a widely used polysaccharide adhesive for bonding cellulosic substrates (Sulaiman et al., 2018). Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2019) evaluated the adhesion properties of dialdehyde cellulose (DAC) wood adhesives with various degrees of oxidation and concentrations in water. Shear strength of the adhesive containing 40 % DAC with a degree of oxidation of 0.78 bonded to beech (Fagus sylvatica) wood was found to be 3.18 MPa, and maximized to 9.53 MPa using DAC with a degree of oxidation of 1.75. The unmodified bacterial polysaccharide FucoPol was also introduced as an adhesive for bonding various materials such as wood, cardboard, glass, and cellulose acetate film with shear strengths of 742, 416, 115.1 and 153.7 kPa, respectively (Araújo et al., 2016).

Natural gums also fall into the category of polysaccharides, mainly used as thickeners and colloid stabilizing agents (Abbasi, 2017). Due to their high hydroxyl content, natural gums could also be utilized as binders in dental, paper, and biomedical adhesives (Dabestani et al., 2018). Utilization of various natural gums such as locust bean gum, Arabic gum, xanthan gum, etc. as natural adhesives dates back to ancient times (Parija et al., 2001). Locust bean gum, guar gum, xanthan gum, and tamarind gum were used as wood adhesives in the laboratory scale (Norström et al., 2014). The results showed that the locust bean gum possessed a shear strength comparable to that of commercial poly(vinyl acetate)-based wood adhesive. Alawode et al. (Alawode et al., 2019) introduced seed kernel extract of Irvingia tree as natural wood adhesives. The shear strength of the extract in a plywood construction was in the range of 0.55–1.7 MPa based on the extraction method and the species of Irvingia tree.

Persian gum (PG) (also called Zedo gum or Farsi gum), a natural polysaccharide mainly native to Iran, is obtained from wild almond trees (Fig. 1 a) (Dabestani et al., 2018; Mohammadi et al., 2016; Samari-Khalaj and Abbasi, 2017) and has been studied systematically during the past few years (Abbasi, 2019, 2017; Dabestani et al., 2018; Hadian et al., 2017). It is a semi-transparent odorless exudate, containing a small amount of lipids and proteins and 82−92 wt. % polysaccharides, mainly composed of arabinose and galactose with the ratio of 2:1 (Abbasi, 2019; Mohammadi et al., 2016) (Fig. 1b). PG, with annual production of 400 metric tons (Dabestani et al., 2018) and the current price of about 2 USD per kilogram, is commercially available in various colors, from white to yellow and red. The lighter the color, the higher the molecular weight and the lower the polydispersity index (Fadavi et al., 2014). According to the proposed chemical structure, the abundant amounts of hydroxyl groups in PG, as in any other polysaccharides such as scleroglucan, starch, and cellulose, lead to inter and intramolecular hydrogen bonding interactions (Bozoğlan et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020).

Despite the reported usage of PG in many applications such as food industry (Abbasi, 2017; Mousazadeh et al., 2018), pharmaceuticals (Abbasi, 2017), soil stabilization (Ghasemzadeh and Modiri, 2020), and wound dressing (Amirsadeghi et al., 2021), etc. its utilization as an adhesive has not been disclosed in the literature. Hence, the objectives of the current research include: 1) introducing the application of PG in the adhesive industry, 2) substituting a major content of the water-based synthetic polymer with PG as a renewable material with the aim of sustainable development in the adhesive industry, 3) making acrylic adhesives water-redispersible, and 4) producing powderable easy-to-use adhesive. To the authors’ best knowledge, this is the first report on preparation of gum-based powder adhesives, performed by taking advantage of the drawback of polysaccharide adhesives, namely low water resistance. The acrylic adhesive was synthesized through emulsion copolymerization and blended with the PG solution in water in various combinations to prepare powderable adhesives. The microstructure, swelling behavior, physicochemical aspects, and adhesion strength of the PG-containing adhesives were studied thoroughly.

Butyl acrylate (BA) and methyl methacrylate (MMA) were purchased from Samchun Pure Chemical Co., Korea. Yellow PG was collected from mountain almond tree in Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari province of Iran. Potassium hydroxide (KOH), sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), tertiary dodecyl mercaptan (TDM) and potassium persulfate (KPS) were purchased from Merck Co., Germany, and used without further purification. The distilled water was obtained from Zolal Teb Shimi Co., Iran.

Poly(methyl methacrylate-co-butyl acrylate) containing 30 wt.% methyl methacrylate (MBC) and poly(butyl acrylate) homopolymer were synthesized through batch emulsion polymerization using the prescribed recipes (Tables 1 and A1, respectively) (Ghasemirad and Mohammadi, 2015). Separate aqueous solutions of SDS and KOH were put into a one-liter four-necked glass reactor equipped with a mechanical stirrer. As the temperature reached 80 °C, the monomer(s), TDM, and aqueous solution of KPS were fed into the reactor. The reaction was completed at 80 °C by agitating the mixture at the speed of 250 rpm using a propeller impeller for 4.5 h (Ghasemirad and Mohammadi, 2015).

The average particle size and polydispersity index of MBC latex were 198 nm and 0.174, respectively, being indicative of a relatively narrow distribution of particles size (Fig. A1). The number-average molecular weight, weight-average molecular weight, and dispersity index of MBC were 9.33 × 104 g/mol, 2.53 × 105 g/mol, and 2.71, respectively. Glass transition temperature of MBC was −22 °C, indicative of its rubbery state at room temperature (Fig. A2).

In order to prepare PG-containing blends, yellow PG powder was dissolved in water at a concentration of 11 wt. % at 50 °C using a magnetic stirrer at 500 rpm for 12 h. The MBC-PG blends were prepared at weight proportions of 100:0, 70:30, 60:40, 55:45, 50:50, 40:60, 30:70, 10:90, and 0:100. The blending was performed by mixing the PG dispersion with MBC latex for 5 min at 25 °C using a magnetic stirrer. All formulations were cast in Teflon molds and dried at room temperature for 30 h. The samples were designated with the type of polymer used in the formulation, i.e., MBC or PBA, followed by PG alphabets and digit(s) standing for PG content based on wt. %.

To measure the moisture content, a certain amount of the PG powder was placed in an oven at 105 °C for 5 h. The moisture content was calculated by dividing the amount of weight loss by the sample initial weight. To measure the amount of total ash, a certain amount of the PG powder was placed in a furnace at 700 °C for 5 h. The total ash content was calculated by dividing the weight of the remaining ash by the initial weight. The experiments for determination of the moisture and ash contents were repeated three times. To determine the amount of fat, 1 g of the dried PG powder was placed in a Soxhlet apparatus and the fat of PG was extracted using normal hexane at 70 °C for 8 h. The fat content was calculated by dividing the amount of extract weight by the sample initial weight. The protein content was analyzed by Kjeldahl nitrogen determination method, being calculated using a conversion factor of 6.25 (Sibaja-Hernández et al., 2015).

Particle size and polydispersity index of the diluted MBC latex were measured by dynamic light scattering (DLS) technique using Zetasizer Nano Series (Malvern Instruments, UK), equipped with a 10 mW HeNe-laser with a wavelength of 633 nm. Measurements were carried out at a detection angle of 173 ° backscattering at 25 °C.
DSC thermogram was obtained for MBC using Mettler Toledo DSC1 instrument (Switzerland) in a heat-cool-heat cycle from -100 to 150 °C at a rate of 10 °C/min under nitrogen purging rate of 80 mL/min.

In order to prepare a suitable sample of PG for GPC analysis, PG powder was poured into a 0.1 M NaNO3 solution in water and allowed to stand overnight. It was then stirred for one hour at 60 °C using a magnetic stirrer. In order to separate the insoluble fractions, the solution was run through a 0.45 μm Millipore filter prior to injection. The molecular weight and dispersity index of PG were determined at 35 °C on a Shimadzu LC-20A GPC (Shimadzu, Japan) equipped with Ultrahydrogel linear columns and a refractometer. 0.1 M NaNO3 aqueous solution was used as an eluent at a flow rate of 1 mL/min.

Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was performed on a Perkin-Elmer Frontier Spectrometer (USA) on pellets made of mixture of each sample and potassium bromide in the wavenumber range of 4000−400 cm−1 with a resolution of 4 cm−1.

Scanning electron microscopy was performed on gold-coated cross section of the blend films samples using SERON TECHNOLOGY AIS-2100 SEM instrument (Korea) at an acceleration voltage of 20 kV under argon gas at room temperature.

It should be noted that this composition was selected due to entirely unswellable nature of pristine acrylic adhesive in water, required for comparison.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Adhesion strength of the PG-containing blends
ce:section.ce:para:
The adhesion strengths were determined by lap shear tests on cotton fabric and beech (Fagus sylvatica) wood. The substrates were rectangular pieces, 10 cm in length and 2.5 cm in width, according to ASTM D1002. In order to prepare adhesive joints, pressure-sensitive adhesive films made of the pristine acrylic polymer or 0.1 g powdered PG-containing adhesives were placed between two pieces of similar substrates forming a contact area of 25 × 25 mm2. Prior to bringing the pieces of substrates into contact, 0.15 g water was sprayed on the powdered adhesives. After being pressed at room temperature by a 20 N load for 1 min, the joint was dried at 60 °C for 2 h. It is worth noting that the joints were dried unpressed, in order to ensure consumer ease of use in the future. The lap shear force was then measured at 24 °C and 15 % relative humidity (RH) using a homemade machine equipped with 1 kN load cell at the strain rate of 1 mm/min. ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of PG, MBC, and the MBC-PG blends
ce:section.ce:para:
PG contained 9 ± 0.25 wt. % moisture and 91 ± 0.25 wt. % dry matter. The percentage of total ash, protein, and fat of PG were found to be 2.9 ± 0.1 wt. %, 0.207 wt. %, and 0.35 wt. %, respectively. The percentage of total sugar of PG was calculated using the formula: 100-(moisture + fat + protein + ash) (Feizollahi et al., 2018), which was found to be 87.543 wt. % (96.2 wt. % based on the dry matter). GPC chromatogram obtained for PG is shown in Fig. 2 . The number-average molecular weight (Mn), weight-average molecular weight (Mw
) , and dispersity index (Đ) of PG were found to be 3.919 × 105 g/mol, 1.917 × 106 g/mol, and 4.892, respectively. To be precise, PG was composed of two low and high molecular weight fractions with characteristics tabulated in Table 2 .

The infrared spectra of the dried MBC adhesive, PG powder, and MBC-PGx blends were shown in Fig. 3 . The broad band observed in the range of 3100 to 2800 cm−1 in the spectrum of MBC adhesive was attributed to the stretching of CH bonds present in CH2 and CH3 groups in MMA and BA monomers (Jingshui et al., 2013). The peak appeared at 1730 cm-1 represented the stretching of carbonyl groups in both monomers. The observed peaks at 1445, 1383, 1245, and 1161 cm-1 were attributed to the stretching of CH in OCH2 and OCH3 and symmetric and asymmetric stretching of COC groups (Monroy-Barreto et al., 2012), respectively. The broad band in the range of 3700 to 3000 and the peak at 623 cm-1 in the spectra of PG were assigned to the stretching and out-of-plane bending of OH groups (Paluszkiewicz et al., 2011). The peaks appeared at 2930 and 1430 cm−1 were attributed to the stretching and bending of CH bonds in CH2 groups. The peaks in the range of 1100 to 1000 cm−1 were assigned to the stretching vibrations of CO and CC groups (Valentin et al., 2007). The band located at 1150 cm−1 was related to the asymmetric vibrations of CO in oxygen bridge (Paluszkiewicz et al., 2011). All PG-containing samples represented a moderately strong band within the range of 1620 to 1600 cm-1 which was attributed to the intra-molecular hydrogen bonds or carboxyl groups of uronic acid (Rezaei et al., 2016). In the blends containing 30, 40, and 45 wt. % of PG, two peaks appeared in the range of 3000 to 3800 cm-1 at 3300 and 3600 cm-1, which were attributed to hydrogen-bonded and free OH groups, respectively (Wallace et al., 2000). The intensified hydrogen bonding in MBC-PG50 and MBC-PG60 was proved by appearance of a broad peak at 3433 cm-1. Narrowing of the strong band at 1737 cm-1 was also indicative of the orientation of MBC carboxyl groups owing to their hydrogen bonding with hydroxyl groups in PG (Ghorbani et al., 2016; Honma et al., 2003; Van der Schueren et al., 2012). The evolving narrowing of the band at 1737 cm-1 from the pristine MBC toward MBC-PG60 further confirmed enhanced hydrogen bonding between the OH groups in PG and carboxyl groups in MBC.

The 1H and 13C-NMR spectrums of PG are shown in Fig. 4 . In the 1H-NMR spectrum (Fig. 4a), the signals appeared in the range of 5−6 ppm (Hz/MHz) and 4−5 ppm were attributed to α-anomeric and β-anomeric protons, respectively (Abbasi, 2017; Stephen et al., 2016). In the 13C-NMR spectrum (Fig. 4b), the signals in the region of 100−105 ppm and 105−110 ppm were assigned to α-anomeric and β-anomeric carbons, respectively (Abbasi, 2017; Stephen et al., 2016). In both of these spectra, the higher intensity of the signals corresponding to β-anomeric in comparison with α-anomeric configuration demonstrated the dominance of β links amongst the building blocks of PG (Abbasi, 2017). The signal appeared in the range of 1.0–1.1 ppm in the 1H-NMR spectrum was attributed to the methyl group protons of rhamnose. The obtained results were in accordance with Abbasi’s thorough investigations on PG structure, which revealed the existence of (1→3) linked β-D-Galp and rhamnose residues in the backbone of PG, and presence of (1→6) linked β-D-Galp, (1→3) linked α-L-Araf, and terminal α-L-Araf in the branches (Abbasi, 2017).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Microstructure and morphology of the MBC-PG blends
ce:section.ce:para: SEM images of the fractured surfaces of MBC-PGx blends are shown in Fig. 5 . PG and MBC appeared in light and dark colors, respectively. In these blends, due to its higher viscosity, PG acted as the dispersed phase and MBC was the continuous phase. A similar morphology was observed in polycaprolactone/chitosan blends containing 10–50 wt. % chitosan, with polycaprolactone acting as the continuous phase, because of its lower viscosity compared to the chitosan (Ghorbani et al., 2016). Here, in low-PG content blends, PG agglomerates were homogeneously distributed in MBC (Fig. 5a and b). Although hydrogen bonds between PG and MBC chains were strong enough to prevent coalescence of the dispersed phase, they were weak to ensure molecular miscibility of the phases. However, further increase in the PG content resulted in appearance of more homogeneously dispersed and distributed PG in the film (Fig. 5c and d). In other words, despite the expectation that phase separation of PG and MBC should have been aggravated with increase in the PG content, the blends evolved toward miscibility due to the enhanced number of intermolecular hydrogen bonds between hydroxyl groups in PG and carbonyl groups in MBC, in accordance with FTIR results.

This diffusion mechanism occurs when polymer chains relaxation rate is much faster than water diffusion rate (Ou et al., 2017). The pseudo-Fickian diffusion of water in MBC-PG slabs was attributed to the high content of MBC in the blend formulations, which had a hydrophobic nature on the one hand and was above its glass transition temperature on the other hand. The solubility parameters of MBC were estimated using the rule of mixtures based on a copolymer containing the overall content of 30 wt. % PMMA and 70 wt. % PBA.

Using the obtained Hansen solubility parameters, the binary interaction parameter for each pair of components in the system (water-PG, water-MBC, and PG-MBC) was calculated using Eqs. (6) & (5) (Table 4 ). The lower binary interaction parameter of water-PG indicated a better compatibility of this system compared to water-MBC and PG-MBC, due to their closer Hildebrand solubility parameters.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Adhesion performance of the MBC-PG blends
ce:section.ce:para: Wetting of a substrate by an adhesive is a prerequisite for occurrence of a proper adhesion. Hence, formulations with low ternary interaction parameters showing easy swelling by water, namely MBC-PG blends containing more than 50 wt. % PG, were introduced as water-redispersible blends, suitable for usage as powder adhesives. The powderability of these formulations stemmed from the high amount of glassy PG content in the system. Lap shear strengths of the MBC-PGx blend adhesives were accordingly evaluated on textile and wood substrates (Fig. 8 a and b). It should be noted that besides reporting the data for powder adhesives, the adhesion strengths of the lower-PG containing blend adhesives (PG-MBC30 and PG-MBC45) were also presented for comparison. The adhesion strength of the pristine PG powder to wood and cotton fabric substrates was measured to be 725 and 359 kPa, respectively. The measured values were approximately equal to and greater than the adhesion strength of FucoPol to wood and cellulose acetate substrates, respectively (Araújo et al., 2016). Adhesion strength of PG powder to wood was also higher than that of Irvingia wombolu kernel extract, obtained by sodium metabisulphite extraction process (Alawode et al., 2019). It is worth mentioning that in all reports in the literature, the physical state of the bio-based adhesives have been liquid, which guarantees the penetration of the adhesive into the substrate, resulting in a high adhesion strength after drying. While herein, a small amount of water sprayed on the powder adhesive triggered its adhesion to the substrate. Moreover, in all previous works the joints were dried pressed, while in the current study they were dried unpressed for ensuring the user-friendliness.

As the adhesion strength of the pristine PG to the cellulosic substrates was higher than that of the pristine MBC, the general trend of change in the adhesion strength of the blends to both substrates was inclining with enhancement in the PG content. It could be attributed not only to more favorable interactions of PG with the cellulosic substrates through significant hydrogen bonds, but also to the cohesive strength of PG compared to the MBC. It is noteworthy that the adhesion strength of MBC-PG90 was higher even than that of the pristine PG to both substrates (765 and 411 kPa for bonding wood and cotton fabric, respectively), which was assigned to the toughening function of 10 wt. % rubbery MBC in the blend. Indeed, the enhanced viscoelastic dissipation of MBC-PG90 compared to the pristine PG boosted the adhesion strength of the adhesive. The general trend of change in the adhesion strength of MBC-PGx was inclining with enhanced water-redispersiblity. However, despite the higher water-redispersiblity of MPC-PG30 than MBC-PG45 (Fig. 6), the former demonstrated lower adhesion strength than the latter. It was assigned to the enhanced hydroxyl group content in the latter with the ability to hydrogen bond with the substrate. The adhesion strengths of the adhesives were higher to the wood substrates (Fig. 8b), than to the fabric substrates (Fig. 8a). It could be attributed to the presence of macroscopic pores on the surface of the fabric in comparison to the microscopic pores on the surface of the wood, which consequently led to the reduction in interfacial area of the adhesive and the substrate and hence declined the adhesion strength. A similar trend of change was also observed in the adhesion strength of the PBA-PG adhesives to the cellulosic substrates as a function of the PG content (Fig. A3), though with lower values than the MBC-PG adhesives, which was a result of the higher cohesive strength of MBC than that of PBA due to the presence of 30 wt. % MMA.

It is worth mentioning that the pristine PG could be utilized as an edible strong adhesive, suitable for children crafting or in food applications. Furthermore, PG could be blended with soft water-incompatible acrylic polymer to make it water-redispersible at a wide range of concentrations and to turn it into a powderable strong adhesive at high PG contents, which results in consumer’s ease of use, appropriate for woodcraft or creating temporary bonds prior to sewing. Adhesion of the non-sticky powdered blend could be activated by being sprayed by water, and the final strong structure could be debonded by injecting water into the joint and reshaped into a new structure using the same adhesive remained on the joint.

Thermal stability of the pristine PG and MBC-PG60, as a representative of the blend adhesives, was measured and shown in Fig. 9 . The thermal behavior of PG resembled that of other gums (Zohuriaan and Shokrolahi, 2004), with a two-stage heat degradation pattern. The first stage of weight loss occurred in the temperature range of 60−130 °C, which was attributed to the removal of moisture hydrogen-bonded to the polysaccharide chains (Zohuriaan and Shokrolahi, 2004). The second stage in the temperature range of 246−400 °C was assigned to the rapid degradation of PG polysaccharide chains. The temperature range of weight loss of MBC-PG60 was similar to that of PG. However, the weight loss due to moisture removal from MBC-PG60 was less than that from the pristine PG (6% and 11 % for MBC-PG60 and PG, respectively). This was a result of the higher hydrophobicity of the acrylic polymer than PG that improved the water-resistance of the blend. Furthermore, MBC-PG60 demonstrated lower weight loss at all temperatures up to about 380 °C compared to PG, indicating the higher thermal stability of the blend adhesive. Increase in the thermal stability of starch-based adhesives using synthetic polymers has been reported in the literature (Zhang et al., 2015). Finally, the residual weight of PG and MBC-PG60 were approximately 11.7 and 7.7 %, respectively. The thermal resistance of the adhesives studied herein was comparable to that of starch-based adhesives reported in the literature (Chen et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015), confirming the high potentiality of PG for use in the wood adhesive industry.

FTIR and SEM results demonstrated developed miscibility between PG and MBC with increase in the PG content in the MBC-PG blends, as a result of the intensified hydrogen bonding in the system. The blends containing more than 50 wt. % PG could be powdered and redispersed in water, following a pseudo-Fickian mechanism in swelling behavior. The equilibrium swelling ratio, Q , increased from MBC to MBC-PG30, decreased from MBC-PG30 to MBC-PG45, and again increased from MBC-PG50 to MBC-PG60.
